lessons.unit: Spring 1: Challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world: the First World War
lessons.title: The modern world and why war broke out in 1914
lessons.bigQuestion: Was the assassination in Sarajevo the main cause of the First World War?
objectives: To understand the long-term and short-term causes of the First World War
successCriteria: All: name the two alliances and the four long-term causes (MAIN)
Most: explain how the assassination led to a wider war
Some: judge which cause was most important
lessons.smsc: Moral: the dangers of pride and rivalry between nations

keywords.def: an agreement between countries to support each other
building up armed forces and trusting in military power
building and competing for empires
strong pride in, and loyalty to, one's nation
the murder of an important person

hook.text: If two friends promised to defend each other in any fight, how could a small argument turn into a big one?

islamicLink.text: Allah says He made people into nations and tribes so that they may know one another, and that the most honoured are the most God-conscious, not the proudest nation (al-Hujurat 49:13). Extreme nationalism, one of the causes of 1914, goes against this teaching.

starter.a: Many lands ruled by one country or ruler
options: Many lands ruled by one country or ruler

starter.q: Which came first: the Industrial Revolution or the First World War?

teach.heading: The big picture
bullets: 1900: European empires ruled much of the world
teach.note: Hodder 8.1 sets the scene: the modern world, empires and industry.

teach.heading: Two alliances
bullets: Italy later joined the other side
teach.note: Use the map of Europe in 1914.

teach.heading: MAIN: long-term causes
bullets: Nationalism: pride and tension, especially in the Balkans
teach.note: Britain and Germany raced to build Dreadnought battleships after 1906.

teach.heading: The spark: summer 1914
teach.note: Walk through the dominoes.

timeline.label: 28 June
timeline.text: Archduke Franz Ferdinand killed in Sarajevo

timeline.label: 4 Aug
timeline.text: Germany invades Belgium; Britain declares war

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Why did Britain declare war on 4 August 1914?
check.why: Britain had promised in 1839 to protect Belgium's neutrality.

practice.q: Explain how alliances turned a local crisis into a world war.
practice.a: Each country was bound to support its allies, so when Austria-Hungary attacked Serbia, Russia, Germany, France and Britain were drawn in
practice.model:
Start: Austria-Hungary attacks Serbia.
Alliance link: Russia backs Serbia; Germany backs Austria-Hungary.
Next: France backs Russia; Germany invades Belgium; Britain joins.
So alliances spread the war.

practice.q: What does the A in MAIN stand for?
practice.a: Alliances

practice.q: Who was assassinated in Sarajevo?
practice.a: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary

independent.q: Core: In the portal response box, write two PEEL paragraphs: one long-term cause and the assassination.
independent.a: Paragraph 1 on a MAIN cause with evidence; paragraph 2 on the assassination as the trigger, explained
independent.model: Teacher goes through paragraph 1: 'Militarism was a long-term cause (P). Britain and Germany raced to build battleships (E). This made each fear the other and ready to fight (E). So war became more likely (L).'

independent.q: Extend: Add a judgement: which cause was most important and why?
independent.a: For example: alliances, because they turned a regional crisis into a world war

independent.q: Stretch: Why is the assassination called a 'trigger' and not the main cause?
independent.a: It started the chain, but the deeper tensions made a big war possible

exit.q: Britain declared war on:
exit.a: 4 August 1914

exit.q: Big question: was the assassination in Sarajevo the main cause of the First World War?
exit.a: It was the trigger; the main causes were long-term: militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism

lessons.homework: Complete Hodder Worksheet 8.1 (the modern world) or the portal version.
lessons.send: SEND: MAIN cards and PEEL frame. EAL: glossary of MAIN words. Stretch: research the 1839 Treaty of London.

PEEL paragraph frame (portal printable)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world: the First World War
lessons.title: 'Your country needs you!': recruitment and propaganda
lessons.bigQuestion: Why did so many young men volunteer to fight in 1914?
objectives: To understand how Britain recruited soldiers and used propaganda in the First World War
successCriteria: All: say what propaganda is
Most: explain three reasons men volunteered
Some: explain why conscription was introduced in 1916
lessons.smsc: Moral: truth, persuasion and freedom of conscience

keywords.def: information used to persuade people, often one-sided
getting people to join the armed forces
someone who chooses to join
the law making people join the armed forces
someone who refuses to fight because of belief

hook.text: If a poster told you your country needed you, what would make you believe it?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'It is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything he hears' (Sahih Muslim). Allah tells us to verify news before acting on it (al-Hujurat 49:6). Propaganda shows why Muslims must check what they are told.

starter.q: MAIN stands for militarism, alliances, imperialism and:
Which country did Germany invade, bringing Britain in?

teach.heading: A call for volunteers
bullets: Britain had a small army in 1914
Hundreds of thousands joined in weeks
teach.note: Kitchener was Secretary of State for War. About 750,000 had joined by the end of September 1914.

teach.heading: Why did men join?
teach.note: Pupils give letters and columns.

teach.heading: Propaganda
teach.note: We describe posters without showing faces. The Defence of the Realm Act (1914) let the government censor news.

model.problem: How does a recruitment poster persuade?
steps: Who made it: the government or a supporter
Message: duty, guilt or pride
Technique: pointing, direct 'you', simple slogan
What it leaves out: the danger and the dead
model.answer: It persuades through emotion and leaves out the cost of war.

teach.heading: From volunteers to conscription
teach.note: Married men were added later in 1916. About 16,000 men were conscientious objectors.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: Volunteers chose; conscripts were required by law; objectors refused.

practice.q: Give three reasons men volunteered in 1914.
practice.a: For example: duty to defend Belgium and Britain, joining with friends, wages and adventure
practice.model:
One from each column:
Duty: defend Belgium.
Pressure: posters and shaming.
Personal: join with friends.
That gives three reasons.

practice.q: Why did the government censor news?
practice.a: To keep up morale and recruitment by hiding bad news

practice.q: Why was conscription introduced in 1916?
practice.a: Not enough men were volunteering after heavy losses

independent.q: Core: In the portal response box, write a PEEL paragraph: 'The main reason men volunteered in 1914 was ...'
independent.a: A clear point with evidence (for example, Pals battalions, Kitchener's call, Belgium) and explanation
independent.model: Teacher goes through it first: 'The main reason was a sense of duty (P). Germany had invaded Belgium, and Kitchener called for volunteers (E). Men believed defending their country was right (E). So duty explains the rush to join (L).'

independent.q: Extend: How reliable are recruitment posters as evidence of why men joined?
independent.a: They show what the government wanted men to feel, not what men actually felt

independent.q: Stretch: Should conscientious objectors have been punished? Give a view.
independent.a: Reasoned view on freedom of belief versus national need

exit.q: Propaganda is:
exit.a: One-sided information to persuade

exit.q: Big question: why did so many young men volunteer to fight in 1914?
exit.a: Duty, propaganda and social pressure, friends joining together, wages and the belief it would be short

lessons.homework: Complete Hodder Worksheet 8.2A.1 (recruitment) or the portal version.
lessons.send: SEND: reasons cards and PEEL frame. EAL: glossary: volunteer, poster, law. Stretch: research the Pals battalions.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world: the First World War
lessons.title: Living and fighting on the Western Front; shell shock
lessons.bigQuestion: What was the hardest part of life on the Western Front?
objectives: To understand conditions on the Western Front and the effects of trench warfare on soldiers
successCriteria: All: describe the layout of a trench system
Most: describe three hardships of trench life
Some: explain why the Somme and shell shock changed attitudes to the war
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: the body and mind under stress
lessons.smsc: Moral: compassion for those with mental injury

keywords.def: the line of trenches through Belgium and France
a deep ditch where soldiers lived and fought
the ground between the two front lines
the term used then for mental injury caused by war
when neither side can win

hook.text: What would you find hardest about living in a muddy ditch for weeks?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss of wealth and lives, but give good news to the patient' (al-Baqarah 2:155). Islam teaches compassion for those who suffer in body or mind; the Prophet, peace be upon him, told Muslims to visit the sick (Sahih al-Bukhari).

teach.heading: Why trenches?
bullets: A line from the Channel to Switzerland
teach.note: By late 1914 a stalemate had set in.

teach.heading: The trench system
bullets: Front line, support and reserve trenches
No Man's Land and barbed wire between
teach.note: Draw it from above as a zigzag. Zigzags stopped blasts travelling along.

teach.heading: Daily life
bullets: Trench foot from cold, wet feet
teach.note: Soldiers rotated: days in the front line, then rest behind the lines.

teach.heading: The Somme and shell shock
bullets: Over 19,000 British soldiers killed on day one
teach.note: The British Army had about 57,000 casualties on the first day. 'Shell shock' was poorly understood; some men were wrongly treated as cowards.

misconception.right: It was a real mental injury caused by the stress and horror of war

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

options: The ground between the two front lines
check.why: It lay between the enemy front lines and was very dangerous to cross.

practice.q: Describe three hardships of trench life.
practice.a: For example: mud and cold, rats and lice, constant danger of shells and snipers
practice.model:
Think of the body, the place and the danger.
Body: trench foot.
Place: mud, rats, lice.
Danger: shells and snipers.
Three hardships.

practice.q: Why were trenches dug in a zigzag?
practice.a: To stop blasts and attackers travelling along the trench

practice.q: Why was shell shock misunderstood?
practice.a: Mental injury was not well understood; some thought it was cowardice

independent.q: Core: Draw a labelled bird's-eye diagram of a trench system with six features and one fact about each.
independent.a: Front, support, reserve and communication trenches, barbed wire, No Man's Land, each with a fact
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: a zigzag line labelled 'front-line trench: soldiers on watch', with barbed wire in front.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box: 'What was the hardest part of trench life?' Give a reasoned answer.
independent.a: Reasoned answer, for example constant fear of shelling, linked to shell shock

independent.q: Stretch: How did the Somme change how people at home saw the war?
independent.a: Huge losses, including whole Pals battalions from one town, shocked people and ended hopes of a quick victory

exit.q: The Battle of the Somme began on:
exit.a: 1 July 1916

exit.q: Big question: what was the hardest part of life on the Western Front?
exit.a: Reasoned answer: mud, disease, boredom, fear and the mental strain that caused shell shock

lessons.homework: Complete Hodder Worksheet 8.2B (the Western Front) or the portal version.
lessons.send: SEND: trench diagram with labels to place. EAL: mud, rat, wire, shell. Stretch: research how treatment of shell shock changed by 1918.
resources: Understanding History: Key Stage 3 (Hodder, 2019) scheme of work, Unit 8, lesson 8.2B Living and fighting on the Western Front (Worksheet 8.2B)
Western Front map (portal printable)
Trench system diagram sheet (portal printable)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world: the First World War
lessons.title: A world war: the Indian Army and Muslim soldiers
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is it called a world war, and whose stories are often forgotten?
objectives: To understand the global nature of the First World War and the contribution of soldiers from the Empire, including Muslims
successCriteria: All: name three places outside Europe where the war was fought
Most: describe the Indian Army's role
Some: explain why these contributions were overlooked and why they matter
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the Muslim contribution to British history

keywords.def: the army of British-ruled India
a peninsula in Turkey where Allied forces fought in 1915
the old name for the land of today's Iraq
Britain's highest award for bravery in battle
the Muslim empire ruled from Istanbul, allied to Germany

hook.text: If your great-grandfather fought in a war, how would you feel if no one remembered him?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Do not diminish people's due' (Hud 11:85). Remembering everyone who served, including Muslim soldiers, is a matter of justice. Muslim soldiers kept their prayers and food rules even at war, and were buried with Islamic rites at Woking.

teach.heading: A global war
teach.note: The Ottoman Empire joined Germany in late 1914, bringing war to the Middle East.

teach.heading: The Indian Army
bullets: Fought in France, Gallipoli, Mesopotamia, East Africa
teach.note: Indian troops arrived in France in autumn 1914, when the British Army badly needed men.

timeline.label: Oct 1914
timeline.text: Indian troops fighting in France and Belgium

timeline.label: 31 Oct 1914
timeline.text: Khudadad Khan's bravery wins the Victoria Cross

teach.heading: Khudadad Khan
bullets: Kept his machine gun firing at Hollebeke, Belgium
First Indian soldier awarded the Victoria Cross
teach.note: No pictures of him: we tell his story in words.

teach.heading: Faith in the field
bullets: A Muslim burial ground built there in 1917
teach.note: Wounded Indian soldiers were treated in Brighton, including at the Royal Pavilion. Woking already had the Shah Jahan Mosque.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Khudadad Khan was the first Indian soldier to receive:
check.why: He won the Victoria Cross for bravery at Hollebeke in October 1914.

practice.q: Why is it called a 'world' war?
practice.a: It was fought on several continents and seas, with soldiers from empires across the world
practice.model:
Where: Europe, the Middle East, Africa, the seas.
Who: soldiers from Britain, France and their empires.
So it was worldwide.

practice.q: Name two places outside Europe where the Indian Army fought.
practice.a: For example: Mesopotamia and East Africa (or Gallipoli)

practice.q: Where is the Muslim burial ground for First World War soldiers in England?
practice.a: Woking, Surrey

independent.q: Core: In the portal response box, write a short biography of Khudadad Khan and explain why his story matters.
independent.a: Muslim soldier from Punjab; bravery at Hollebeke, 31 October 1914; first Indian VC; matters because it shows the Empire's and Muslims' contribution
independent.model: Teacher shows the first sentence: 'Khudadad Khan was a Muslim soldier from Punjab in the Indian Army.'

independent.q: Extend: Why were the contributions of Empire soldiers often overlooked?
independent.a: Histories focused on British soldiers on the Western Front; few records or memorials told their stories

independent.q: Stretch: How can historians recover forgotten stories?
independent.a: Letters, army records, hospital records, memorials and family memories

exit.q: Mesopotamia is today's:
exit.a: Iraq

exit.q: Big question: why is it called a world war, and whose stories are often forgotten?
exit.a: It was fought across the world; the stories of Indian, African and other Empire soldiers, including Muslims, were often forgotten

lessons.homework: Complete Hodder Worksheet 8.2C (the global conflict) or the portal version.
lessons.send: SEND: biography frame. EAL: glossary: soldier, award, brave. Stretch: research the Muslim burial ground at Woking.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world: the First World War
lessons.title: The peace treaty and future problems; unit quiz
lessons.bigQuestion: Did the Treaty of Versailles make another war more likely?
objectives: To understand the terms of the Treaty of Versailles and why it caused future problems
successCriteria: All: name three terms of the Treaty of Versailles
Most: explain why Germany resented the treaty
Some: judge whether the treaty was fair, considering different views
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: new borders in Europe and the Middle East
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice and revenge in making peace

keywords.def: an agreement to stop fighting
a formal agreement between countries
money paid for war damage
blame for causing the war
an organisation set up to keep peace

hook.text: After a fight, what makes a peace last: punishing the loser or treating them fairly?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'If they incline to peace, then incline to it also, and trust in Allah' (al-Anfal 8:61), and commands justice even towards enemies (al-Ma'idah 5:8). A peace built on justice lasts longer than one built on revenge.

starter.q: Why did Britain declare war in 1914?

teach.heading: The end of the war
teach.note: The 'Big Three': Wilson (USA), Lloyd George (Britain), Clemenceau (France).

teach.heading: The Treaty of Versailles, 28 June 1919
bullets: Reparations set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks
Army limited to 100,000; no air force
teach.note: Remember with BRAT: Blame, Reparations, Army, Territory.

teach.heading: Different views
teach.note: Germany was not allowed to take part in the talks. Ask pupils which side of the compare box they find stronger.

teach.heading: The Middle East after the war
teach.note: Britain took Iraq and Palestine; France took Syria and Lebanon. The Ottoman sultanate ended in 1922 and the caliphate was abolished in 1924.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

options: Germany had to accept blame for the war
check.why: War guilt was the clause blaming Germany; reparations were the payments.

practice.q: Explain why Germany resented the treaty.
practice.a: It was blamed for the war, had to pay huge reparations, lost land and its army was cut, without being allowed to negotiate
practice.model:
Use BRAT.
Blame: humiliating.
Reparations: crippling payments.
Army and Territory: weakened.
Not allowed to negotiate: a 'dictated peace'.

practice.q: When was the armistice?
practice.a: 11am, 11 November 1918

practice.q: What happened to Ottoman lands?
practice.a: They were divided, with Britain and France ruling mandates

independent.q: Core: First World War unit quiz on the portal (12 questions: causes, recruitment, Western Front, global war, Versailles).
independent.a: Answers in the portal quiz key
independent.model: Teacher does question 1 aloud: 'What do the letters MAIN stand for?' Militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box: 'The Treaty of Versailles was too harsh.' How far do you agree?
independent.a: Balanced answer: harsh terms caused resentment, but France suffered greatly and Germany kept its core; judgement with reasons

independent.q: Stretch: How did the peace settlement affect the Middle East?
independent.a: Ottoman lands were divided into British and French mandates, creating borders and tensions that lasted

exit.q: Reparations means:
exit.a: Money paid for war damage

exit.q: Big question: did the Treaty of Versailles make another war more likely?
exit.a: Reasoned view: many historians argue resentment helped extremists later, though other factors mattered too

lessons.homework: Revise the First World War with the Hodder Unit 8 summary for the next unit (the Second World War).
lessons.send: SEND: BRAT card; quiz read aloud. EAL: glossary: peace, blame, pay. Stretch: research Sykes-Picot (1916).

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The Second World War, Churchill and the Holocaust
lessons.title: Churchill's career to 1940
lessons.bigQuestion: Should we judge a person by their best moments or their whole life?
objectives: To understand Churchill's career before 1940 and how to judge his significance
successCriteria: All: describe three events in Churchill's career before 1940
Most: assess strengths and weaknesses using criteria
Some: explain why interpretations of Churchill differ

keywords.def: an experienced and respected political leader
giving in to an aggressor's demands to avoid war
the minister in charge of the economy
Churchill's 1930s without a government job
a view of the past

hook.text: Can someone be a hero to one group of people and a villain to another? Think of an example.

starter.q: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in:
Gallipoli was a campaign of the:
Give one term of the Treaty of Versailles.
starter.a: For example: war guilt clause, reparations, army limited to 100,000

teach.heading: Criteria of greatness
teach.note: Agree criteria as a class (Hodder 8.4A).

teach.heading: Early career, 1900 to 1918
bullets: First Lord of the Admiralty; Gallipoli failure, 1915
teach.note: He resigned after Gallipoli and served on the Western Front in 1916.

teach.heading: 1918 to 1940
teach.note: Prime Minister on 10 May 1940.

teach.heading: Summary card
teach.note: Model.

steps: Strength: right about the danger from Hitler
Weakness: opposed Indian self-government
Judgement: good judgement on Germany, poor on India

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

options: Giving in to demands to avoid war
check.why: Britain's 1930s policy gave Hitler concessions, like the Sudetenland in 1938.

practice.q: Explain one reason Churchill's reputation was low in the 1930s. (2 marks)
practice.a: Gallipoli was still blamed on him (1); his views on India seemed out of date to many (1)
practice.model:
Point: past failures.
Evidence: Gallipoli, 1915.
Explain: many doubted his judgement.

independent.q: Core: Make three summary cards (1900 to 1918; 1918 to 1930; 1930 to 1940) with a strength, a weakness and a judgement on each.
independent.a: Three balanced cards

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, explain why some historians criticise Churchill.
independent.a: Gallipoli; views on India and empire; Bengal famine of 1943 (next lesson)

independent.q: Stretch: Was Churchill right about appeasement? Explain.
independent.a: Yes: Hitler broke the Munich Agreement in March 1939

exit.q: Churchill became Prime Minister on:
Big question: best moments or whole life?
exit.a: A balanced view using the whole record and agreed criteria

lessons.homework: Interview a family member: what do they know about Churchill? Compare with what you learned.
lessons.send: SEND: summary card frames. EAL: glossary. Stretch: research Churchill's role in the 1911 Sidney Street siege or the 1910 Tonypandy riots.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The Second World War, Churchill and the Holocaust
lessons.title: War leader: Dunkirk, the Battle of Britain and the Blitz
lessons.bigQuestion: Was the 'Blitz spirit' real or propaganda?
objectives: To understand Britain's survival in 1940 to 1941 and how propaganda shaped memory of the Blitz
successCriteria: All: describe Dunkirk, the Battle of Britain and the Blitz
Most: explain Churchill's role as war leader
Some: evaluate how far the Blitz spirit was a myth

keywords.def: moving people away from danger
the German bombing of British cities, 1940 to 1941
how confident and hopeful people feel
information used to persuade, often one-sided
controlling what can be published

hook.text: Why might a government want people to believe everyone was cheerful during the bombing?

starter.a: Giving in to demands to avoid war
options: Giving in to demands to avoid war

starter.q: Name one failure of Churchill's before 1940.

teach.heading: Dunkirk
teach.note: A defeat turned into a story of survival.

teach.heading: The Battle of Britain
bullets: Radar and the Spitfire and Hurricane
teach.note: Germany failed to win control of the air, so invasion was called off.

teach.heading: The Blitz
teach.note: Churchill's speeches and visits aimed to keep morale high.

teach.heading: Blitz spirit: myth or reality?
bullets: Many showed courage and kept working
teach.note: Hodder 8.5: a famous 1940 London photograph was staged for propaganda (described, not shown).

model.problem: How useful is a staged 1940 photograph for studying the Blitz?
steps: Content: shows normal life going on amid ruins
Origin: taken for a newspaper in 1940
Purpose: to boost morale; it was staged
Judgement: useful for propaganda, not for typical experience
model.answer: Useful for how the government wanted the Blitz seen

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Why did Germany call off the invasion of Britain in 1940?
options: They lost the Battle of Britain
check.why: Without control of the air, an invasion across the Channel was too risky.

practice.q: Explain why the Battle of Britain was important. (4 marks)
practice.a: The RAF stopped the Luftwaffe winning air control (2), so Germany could not invade and Britain stayed in the war (2)
practice.model:
Event: RAF versus Luftwaffe.
Result: no air control for Germany.
Consequence: invasion called off; Britain fights on.

independent.q: Core: In the portal response box: 'How far was the Blitz spirit a myth?' (8 marks) Starter: 'There is some evidence that ... However ...'
independent.a: Balanced: real courage and endurance vs fear, looting, censorship; judgement
independent.model: Teacher plans the answer: two sides plus judgement.

independent.q: Extend: Write the war-leader summary card for Churchill (1940 to 1941).
independent.a: Strengths: speeches, refused to make peace; weaknesses: some costly decisions

independent.q: Stretch: Why are wartime speeches strong evidence of aims but weak evidence of public feeling?
independent.a: They show what leaders wanted people to feel, not what they did feel

exit.q: The Blitz lasted from:
exit.a: September 1940 to May 1941

exit.q: Big question: was the Blitz spirit real or propaganda?
exit.a: Both: real courage existed, but censorship and propaganda exaggerated unity and hid fear

lessons.homework: Use the Imperial War Museum website to find one Blitz object (not a person) and explain what it shows.
lessons.send: SEND: essay frame. EAL: glossary. Stretch: research the Coventry Blitz of November 1940.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The Second World War, Churchill and the Holocaust
lessons.title: A world war: Stalingrad, Pearl Harbor, D-Day and the atomic bombs
lessons.bigQuestion: Which was the real turning point of the Second World War?
objectives: To understand the global turning points of the Second World War
successCriteria: All: place five key events on a timeline
